result:
The town’s lost-and-found occupied a narrow room behind the post office. It contained the usual umbrellas, gloves, and single earrings, but also things nobody could quite explain: a key warm to the touch, a photograph that showed a different sky each morning, a jar labeled **TUESDAY**.

Mara, who managed the room, kept a ledger. Most people came looking for something practical. Once, a man asked whether anyone had turned in his courage. She checked the shelves anyway.

“Not this week,” she said. “But leave your name.”

He returned the following month carrying a suitcase and wearing a coat too thin for the weather. He had come to say goodbye. Mara noticed his hands were shaking as he reached for the door.

“I never found it,” she said.

“That’s all right,” he told her. “I couldn’t wait any longer.”

After he left, Mara opened the ledger and crossed out his name. She considered adding a note, then closed the book without one. Outside, the bus pulled away, and the jar on the shelf gave a small, bright rattle.
